subject: first-amendment
title: The First Amendment: Text, Origins, and a Standard
summary: Why the Bill of Rights was added, and how Tinker built a test for rights inside institutions.

keys.answer: School officials can't ban student expression merely on suspicion of disruption; it calls for case-by-case judgment about actual disruption.

keys.prompt: What's the trade-off between rules and standards?
keys.answer: Rules are predictable and cheap to apply but misfit edge cases; standards fit better but invite inconsistency and litigation.

keys.prompt: Why was a Bill of Rights added at all?
keys.answer: Several state ratifying conventions wanted "declaratory and restrictive clauses" to prevent misconstruction or abuse of federal power.

cards.title: "Article the third"
cards.text: In the twelve amendments Congress sent to the states in 1789, what we call the First Amendment was listed third. Why was there a Bill of Rights at all, and how do courts apply one sentence to the messy reality of institutions?

cards.question: In Tinker (1969), did the Court set a bright-line rule or a case-by-case standard?
cards.reveal: A standard: officials can't ban expression merely on suspicion of disruption, which calls for judgment about actual disruption case by case. More fit, less predictability.

cards.title: Why it was added
cards.text: The congressional resolution proposing the amendments says several state ratifying conventions wanted "further declaratory and restrictive clauses" added "to prevent misconstruction or abuse of its powers." It also hoped to extend "public confidence in the Government." Congress passed the First Amendment on September 25, 1789; it was ratified December 15, 1791.

cards.title: Five clauses
cards.text: One sentence holds distinct clauses: establishment, free exercise, speech, press, and assembly and petition. Each has its own body of interpretation. The text restrains government ("Congress shall make no law…"), not private parties.

why.q: Why doesn't the First Amendment apply to a private company's speech rules?
why.a: Its text restrains government ("Congress shall make no law…"), not private parties.

cards.title: Tinker as a standard
cards.text: Tinker v. Des Moines (7–2, 1969): officials could not ban students' black armbands protesting the Vietnam War merely on suspicion of disruption. That is a standard, not a bright-line rule: it calls for case-by-case judgment about disruption, not mere suspicion of it.
cards.example: The dissent argued that school is for learning, that no one has a right to express any opinion at any time, and that officials need broad authority over order.

cards.title: Rules vs. standards
cards.text: Bright-line rules are predictable and cheap to apply but misfit edge cases. Standards fit cases better but invite inconsistency and litigation. Tinker chose a standard for expression inside an institution with a legitimate mission. The tension recurs in workplaces, campuses, and platforms.

cards.prompt: "Separation of Powers as Incentive Design" was about structure. The Bill of Rights adds enumerated limits. Why might the ratifying conventions have wanted both?
cards.model: Structure makes branches check each other, but conventions still wanted explicit "restrictive clauses" to prevent misconstruction or abuse; a written right gives courts a clear line to enforce.

cards.question: Where do you draw the line between individual expression and an institution's mission, in schools, companies, or online platforms? Would you rather have a rule or a standard, and why?
nudges: Steelman the Tinker dissent before rejecting it.
Which errors are cheaper: allowing too much speech or too little?
